title: Redwood cost economics discovery - Vector Capital
summary: Initial cost/unit economics discovery focused on per-token pricing, batching and caching levers. Vector Capital runs a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline with peak inference spikes for trading signals. Primary concerns: predictable unit cost, latency SLOs during spikes, and data residency for EU customers. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send detailed pricing model and batching recommendations; run a 2-week pilot benchmark on hosted with sample traffic; follow-up technical deep dive focused on Dedicated sizing and VPC networking.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Moore (Vector Capital - Head of MLOps), Sofia Alvarez (Vector CTO), Liam Chen (Vector SRE)

Summary (auto): cost economics, per-token pricing, batching/caching, Dedicated vs Hosted, pilot next steps

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya our systems engineer. How are you all?
[00:08] Ethan: Good, thanks. Sofia and Liam are here as well. We've been doing some homework on hosting options — curious about the per-token math at scale.
[00:16] Sofia: Yeah we need to understand predictable unit cost. We run a RAG pipeline for market signals, heavy spikes around open/close windows.
[00:25] Priya: Got it. Roughly can you share current qps and tokens per request? Even ballparks help steer batching/caching advice.
[00:34] Ethan: Sure, typical steady-state is 30 qps, bursts up to 450 qps for 90 seconds during market events. Avg tokens in requests ~120 input, output ~60. Some requests are much longer — up to 1k tokens when we summarize long documents.
[00:52] Liam: Our infra team worries about tail latency during bursts. If cost optimization adds latency we need to quantify tradeoffs.
[01:04] Jordan: Totally. Our two levers are batching and KV/prefix caching. Batching reduces per-token compute by amortizing scheduler overhead; caching reduces repeated prefix compute for similar prompts. Both can lower unit cost but batching can add a small queuing delay.
[01:20] Priya: For your profile — short-ish avg tokens with frequent repeats — KV cache could be very effective. For spikes, continuous batching with adaptive timeouts is a common pattern: we target sub-20ms additional queuing for latency-sensitive routes and longer windows for background jobs.
[01:37] Sofia: What's the per-token delta between Hosted and Dedicated? We want to see where break-even is.
[01:45] Jordan: Great question. Hosted is usage-based: list example: $0.000016 per prompt-token and $0.000040 per completion-token for larger models — that's illustrative — while Dedicated is committed capacity: typically you pay for reserved GPU pools monthly. Effective per-token can go down 2x-5x depending on utilization and quantization. Important is utilization assumptions — if you only need small base throughput Dedicated can be more expensive unless you commit to high utilization.
[02:10] Ethan: Do you have a model for peak vs average? Our finance needs forcastable spend.
[02:16] Priya: We provide a cost projection spreadsheet, we model three scenarios: steady, bursty with cache, and bursty without cache. Caching often reduces tokens processed by 15-45% depending on repetition. Batching gives more benefit on throughput models — like steady high qps — less on very spiky low-duration bursts.
[02:36] Liam: For Dedicated, do you support autoscaling and burst capacity? We can't have dropped requests during spikes.
[02:42] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated supports autoscale policies and configured burst pools. You can set guaranteed baseline capacity and a burst tier that can be billed on usage; there's an SLA. Fallback routing to hosted variants is also possible if private capacity is exhausted.
[02:55] Sofia: About security — we need VPC, KMS, SOC2, and EU data residency. How does Hosted handle those?
[03:03] Priya: Hosted can support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest via integrations, audit logs, SSO/SAML in enterprise plans, and region-specific hosting for EU data residency. For stricter controls we recommend Private (VPC/on-prem). We'll share our security pack.
[03:18] Ethan: Back to cost: can you explain token accounting? We sometimes see mismatch between how our logs count tokens and vendor billing.
[03:25] Jordan: We bill on model input+output tokenization with a consistent tokenizer per model. Differences can arise from prompt engineering and special tokens. We'll align on tokenization model you use in the pilot. Also note caching reduces billed tokens by avoiding recomputing prefix tokens if results are served from KV cache or earlier cached completions.
[03:46] Sofia: If we run a pilot on Hosted with our traffic, can we expect realistic unit costs?
[03:52] Priya: Yes — pilot benchmarks simulate traffic and measure effective tokens/sec, latency, and unit cost. We typically ask for request traces and a sampling harness. We can run the pilot on Hosted with instrumentation and then extrapolate Dedicated sizing.
[04:06] Ethan: What about model variants and quantization? We sometimes lose quality with aggressive int8 quantization.
[04:13] Jordan: We recommend model/quantization pairings per workload. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization only after A/B tests on metric suites. The cost delta between fp16 and int8 can be significant; we can show expected throughput gains and quality tradeoffs from our past benchmarks.
[04:30] Liam: Networking — if we go Private/VPC, what's the latency hit for cross-region calls to data sources?
[04:36] Priya: It depends. Private deployments colocate near your VPC endpoints; if you need global presence, we can size edge routing or use regional Dedicated clusters. We'll look at the topology when you share infra maps.
[04:49] Jordan: Quick aside: competitors — we often see customers compare us to Inferex and the major clouds. Common decision factors are unit economics at steady state, ease of ops, and fallback reliability.
[04:59] Ethan: Right. Also we have procurement timeline — decision in Q2 if costs look right.
[05:05] Priya: Okay here's a concrete example. If you have 100M tokens/month billed on Hosted at $0.00003/token that's $3k/month. If caching reduces billed tokens by 30% you drop to 70M tokens => $2.1k. If Dedicated results in 3x lower per-token cost at high utilization your equivalent spend could be $1k, plus fixed monthly reservation. Break-even will depend on your committed throughput.
[05:30] Sofia: That helps. Can you share a sensitivity chart?
[05:33] Jordan: We'll send the pricing sheet and sensitivity chart.
[05:36] Ethan: About SLAs — what's guaranteed latency for hosted vs dedicated?
[05:40] Priya: Hosted has best-effort with SLO guidance and dashboards. Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for reserved pools; you can configure SLOs per route.
[05:51] Liam: For our ops, observability and token-level cost breakouts are important. Can we see per-route cost in the console?
[05:58] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model, plus tracing. We can demo that in the next meeting.
[06:06] [silence/background typing]
[06:30] Ethan: One thing — during spikes we generate lots of near-duplicate prompts; how often does caching hit?
[06:36] Priya: In similar use cases we've seen cache hit rates 20-60% depending on prompt churn and RAG similarity. We can tune caching window and fingerprinting. Also prefix KV caches are very effective when a lot of tokens are repeated at the start of requests.
[06:55] Jordan: We'll propose a pilot: 2-week hosted benchmark with your sample traces, Redwood instrumentation, and a joint review. After that we'll size Dedicated options if needed.
[07:06] Sofia: Good. Can that pilot include a run with and without cache/batching so we can see delta?
[07:11] Priya: Absolutely. We'll include three runs: baseline (no caching), caching enabled, and caching+batching optimized.
[07:19] Ethan: Cost accounting during pilot — do you bill us normal usage or is there a pilot credit?
[07:24] Jordan: We usually offer pilot credits for evaluation. We'll detail that in the pricing sheet.
[07:30] Liam: For procurement, we'll need SOC2 and data processing addendum. Can you share standard contracts?
[07:36] Jordan: Yes will include security docs and DPA.
[07:40] [10 minutes of deeper technical Q&A — paraphrased]
[17:45] Priya: If you look at token distribution histogram, you can optimize two buckets: small interactive requests and long-document summarization. For the latter, we recommend chunking and streaming outputs to avoid long tail compute.
[18:05] Ethan: Streaming — does streaming change cost model?
[18:09] Jordan: Billing is still per token produced; streaming doesn't change token billing but can improve perceived latency and let you start delivering partial results. It also enables early cutoff heuristics to save tokens for certain flows.
[18:25] Sofia: On the Dedicated sizing — what's typical GPU mix? A100 vs H100 vs LLM-optimized cards?
[18:32] Priya: Depends on model family. For large open models H100s with nvlink pools are common; for quantized smaller models A100 or even consumer-class Ampere can work. We'll propose a mix based on target throughput and latency SLO.
[18:48] Liam: Any gotchas on request shaping and burst protection?
[18:52] Priya: Rate limiting, circuit breakers, and adaptive batching are the standard controls. Also prefix caching and per-route prioritization so critical routes bypass certain optimizations.
[19:05] Ethan: Great. From finance standpoint we need a 12-month forecast and a break-even analysis.
[19:10] Jordan: We'll include a 12-month forecast in the pricing pack with sensitivity to cache hit rate and utilization.
[19:18] Sofia: What's the expected timeline for setting up a Dedicated cluster if we decide?
[19:22] Priya: Usually 4-8 weeks for Dedicated depending on procurement and whether we need on-prem network integration. Hosted pilot can start within a few days after we get traces.
[19:34] Ethan: Okay that's workable. Any other questions?
[19:38] Liam: Slight question: do you charge for tokenization overhead or embedding ops separately?
[19:44] Jordan: Embeddings billed per embedding unit separately; tokenization itself is part of prompt/completion token billing. We'll call out embeddings on the sheet.
[19:52] [people talk about internal next steps briefly]
[20:10] Jordan: Recap: Jordan will send pricing + pilot credit details; Priya will share batching/caching playbook; Ethan to share traces. We'll schedule a technical deep dive the week of 2026-03-30.
[20:22] Sofia: Sounds good. Thanks Jordan, Priya.
[20:25] Ethan: Thanks everyone.
[20:28] Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up via email with links to security docs and the PRICING spreadsheet.
[20:32] [meeting ends]
notes: Pilot recommended: 2-week hosted benchmark covering baseline, caching, and optimized batching
Key metrics requested from customer: qps profile, token histograms, peak durations
Break-even depends on utilization; supply sensitivity chart in follow-up
